packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still present 15 months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the EU DMA choice-screen mandate rollout across iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest evidence available that a mandated active-choice screen produces large, durable behavior change away from a default in a mobile app under EU regulation, directly informing whether active choice at onboarding could substitute for opt-out without the disengagement risk.
limitations: browser default choice rather than a savings/financial decision
no direct measure of amount saved or engagement depth
packets.relevance_reason: Best EU-regulatory precedent for active choice screens producing large, persistent shifts away from defaults in a mobile-app context, directly informing the active-choice option in the entry decision.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, with liquidity-constrained cardholders driving the null result.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with six-month follow-up (NBER working paper).
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests the enrollment-vs-real-outcome distinction in a consumer financial product: behavior changed but the substantive outcome did not, exactly the 'vanity enrollment' concern our support team raised.
limitations: credit card debt paydown differs from savings accumulation
the nudge shrouds an option rather than testing opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing directly
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-financial nudge study separating nominal enrollment change from actual behavioral/financial outcome, the core trade-off in the brief.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the advice received compared to no default, especially when the client refused the default.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the helpful-versus-manipulative trade-off in an EU financial-advice context: even an effective default carries a perceived-honesty cost, bearing on both the entry design and how a preset multiplier should be framed to avoid a dark-pattern read.
limitations: wealth-management investment-risk context rather than round-up savings specifically
outcome measured via advice ratings, not actual retention or saved amounts
packets.relevance_reason: Best available EU evidence on when a financial default is perceived as manipulative, directly addressing the brief's reputational-risk criterion.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when staying costs substantial drug consumption losses.
packets.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options among Medicare Part D beneficiaries.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows self-directed defaults (no employer intermediary) persist and can actively harm passive low-income users who don't reassess a bad default — direct evidence for the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question and for testing whether the employer-trust mechanism is necessary.
limitations: health-insurance domain, not banking/savings
low-income Medicare population differs from general banking-app users
abstract gives no percentage effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: Closest analogue to a self-directed (non-employer) default showing persistence and distributional harm, the exact mechanism gap the brief flags.
packets.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
packets.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults hold at the first escalation date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, withdrawal-on-separation, and auto-escalation opt-out. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: enrollment lift is real at signup but shrinks sharply once attrition, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for — a direct check on the 'defaults reliably lift real saving' premise.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives limited breakdown by demographic subgroup
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise real saving, using quantified effect sizes over the medium-to-long run, exactly what the brief asks to weigh against the 'default everyone in' argument.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Automatic enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out, with the default effect stronger when incentives are high and knowledge of enrollment status is low.
packets.methodology: Natural experiment on nationwide auto-enrollment policy using linked administrative and survey data.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides a clean effect-size estimate of an opt-out default absent an employer intermediary and shows the effect is conditional on incentive salience and consumer knowledge — directly informs how large our own enrollment lift might be and for which users.
limitations: public pension context, not a discretionary consumer savings app
concerns a specifically low-income population
packets.relevance_reason: Quantified default effect and heterogeneity evidence in a government (non-employer) default setting, the closest test of whether the 'trusted intermediary' mechanism is necessary.
packets.title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
packets.abstract: Default settings strongly increase pension enrollment, especially when savings incentives are high and choices are complex. We show that the effect is weaker when incentives are low, options are simple, and opting out is easy. We study the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pay-as-you-go pension system. We find that automatic enrollment raises participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out. Linking administrative and survey data shows that the default effect is stronger when enrollment incentives are higher and among individuals who lack knowledge of their enrollment status.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign sites raised donations by over $43 million while also raising refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller and less experienced donors.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the timing of default rollout across multiple 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
packets.why_it_matters: The best available real-world causal estimate of a default on a recurring financial commitment, including a direct complaint/backfire proxy (refund requests) and evidence the effect falls hardest on inexperienced, small-money users, precisely the disengagement/complaint risk our support team raised.
limitations: political donations rather than a savings product
no direct measure of long-term retention or withdrawal
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available evidence that pre-checked defaults on recurring monetary commitments increase both uptake and complaint-like backlash, disproportionately among smaller/inexperienced users.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework showing that downstream default effects depend on the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience, and identifies gaps and inconsistencies in prior findings.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review and taxonomy synthesizing the consumer default-effect literature, abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict when and why a default's effect on enrollment will or will not persist into engagement and saved amounts — directly informs what to measure over 6-12 months.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical rather than a new empirical estimate
abstract-only, no effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: The synthesis/review the brief calls for on downstream persistence of default effects, applicable across consumer product settings including ours.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, each $1 of subsidy spending (requiring active choice) raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic/passive employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation; ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic contributions, while the wealthier, more sophisticated 15% 'active savers' mainly shift assets across accounts.
packets.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish savings accounts, comparing active-choice tax subsidies to passive/automatic employer contributions.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest available causal evidence that automatic/default mechanisms move actual saved amounts (not just nominal enrollment) far more than active-choice mechanisms, and that the people helped by defaults are exactly the less sophisticated, passive majority — directly bears on whether enrollment lift is 'vanity' and on who benefits from an opt-out design versus active choice.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts, not liquid consumer savings
Denmark's institutional context (mandatory pension infrastructure) differs from an EU consumer banking app
measures subsidy-induced shifting versus automatic contribution, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment design per se
packets.relevance_reason: Provides the clearest large-sample evidence that passive/default mechanisms move real saved amounts and disproportionately help less-sophisticated users, the exact distributional trade-off the brief asks about, even though the setting is retirement accounts.
packets.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
packets.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

packets.key_finding: Synthesizes the behavioral household-finance literature, covering consumption/savings, product design, choice architecture, and disclosure interventions across consumer financial contexts, not solely employer retirement plans.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/chapter summarizing empirical regularities and behavioral interventions in household finance.
packets.why_it_matters: Serves as the review-level synthesis of default and choice-architecture effects in consumer (not just employer) financial settings, giving a broader evidence base and caveats for weighing the enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off than any single study.
limitations: broad narrative overview rather than a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers many topics beyond enrollment defaults, diluting specificity
abstract-only detail on any single finding
packets.relevance_reason: Provides the review/synthesis-level evidence the brief explicitly asks for, framed around consumer (not only employer) financial behavior.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

alternates.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on Chinese voluntary pension saving, all tested nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative framing and default options, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
alternates.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment': here the default option backfired and reduced willingness to contribute, with heterogeneous effects by demographic group, exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked us to surface.
limitations: hypothetical survey-based willingness rather than real enrollment behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not generalize to an EU banking app
small sample (n=220)
alternates.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in this set: a controlled trial where the default-option nudge backfired rather than helped, directly countering the brief's stated internal assumption.
alternates.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
alternates.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
alternates.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

alternates.key_finding: Opt-in enrollment in an employer payroll-deduction liquid, withdraw-anytime savings account produced very low take-up (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees), but among those who enrolled, 96% still had a balance and 87% still received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
alternates.methodology: Field study of a short-term savings choice-architecture program introduced at five U.K. firms, observed over a 12-month window for enrolled users.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest existing evidence for a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings product: opt-in yields very low nominal enrollment but the enrolled minority is highly persistent, directly informing the trade-off between opt-in's small-but-engaged cohort and opt-out's larger-but-possibly-disengaged one.
limitations: employer payroll channel rather than a standalone consumer app
UK setting; no data on withdrawal amounts or complaint rates
alternates.relevance_reason: Nearest available liquid-savings analogue to the round-up product, directly informing the opt-in enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off central to the Entry decision.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of potential savings.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale field experiments across major UK banks on automatic enrollment into an alert feature.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the closest real precedent to our product: a UK bank auto-enrolling customers into a financial-behavior-nudging app feature with measured, economically meaningful effect sizes, directly benchmarking what auto-enrolling users into round-up savings could plausibly achieve.
limitations: alerts, not savings contributions, are the enrolled feature
no multi-year persistence or withdrawal data reported
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest prior work: UK consumer banking app feature with automatic enrollment and measured financial outcomes.
alternates.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
alternates.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions attenuates from 12 months to 36 months, with modest average savings gains at the longer horizon but a significant reduction in savings inequality; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, quantified answer to whether default effects persist at 12-36 months — showing attenuation — directly bearing on whether an opt-out design's enrollment lift will still show up in actual saved amounts a year later.
limitations: employer/national retirement plans, not a discretionary liquid consumer product
switching-cost estimate is model-based rather than directly observed
alternates.relevance_reason: The clearest quantitative evidence on default-effect persistence over exactly the 12+ month horizon the brief asks about.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: A field experiment with payment reminders in a consumer credit card/checking platform in Brazil reduced late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil; heterogeneity analysis by prior overdraft history.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's worry made concrete with numbers: a well-intentioned behavioural nudge in a consumer, self-directed fintech setting can help most users but net-harm a vulnerable subgroup, which is exactly the distributional risk the round-up default decision needs to be checked against before shipping opt-out.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchors, so C1/C3/C6 are not addressed
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a savings round-up feature
single-country (Brazil) fintech platform, generalisability to EU app context untested
alternates.relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence in this batch that a nudge which helps on average can create a net-harmed subgroup in a genuinely consumer, self-directed financial-app setting, directly informing the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk criterion.
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.
